cases.question_text: What are the primary clinical presentations of Wilson's Disease, and which initial physical signs warrant immediate diagnostic evaluation?
expected_answer_elements: Hepatic manifestations (acute hepatitis, chronic liver disease, cirrhosis, hepatomegaly)
Neurological and psychiatric manifestations (tremor, dystonia, dysarthria, behavioral changes)
Ophthalmic signs (Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam, sunflower cataracts)
Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia as an acute diagnostic clue

cases.question_text: Explain the Leipzig scoring system for Wilson disease diagnosis: criteria, point allocation, and interpretation thresholds.
expected_answer_elements: Kayser-Fleischer rings scoring (present: 2, absent: 0)
Neurological symptoms scoring (severe: 2, mild: 1, absent: 0)
Serum ceruloplasmin scoring (<0.1 g/L: 2, 0.1-0.2 g/L: 1, normal: 0)
Liver copper content scoring (>250 µg/g: 2, 50-249 µg/g: 1, normal: -1)
24-hour urinary copper scoring (>2x ULN: 2, 1-2x ULN: 1, normal: 0)
ATP7B mutation analysis (both chromosomes: 2, 1 chromosome: 1, none: 0)
Consensus interpretation cutoffs (>=4: established diagnosis, 2-3: probable, 0-1: unlikely)

cases.question_text: What is the clinical role of serum ceruloplasmin in diagnosing Wilson's Disease, and what factors can cause false-positive or false-negative results?
expected_answer_elements: Standard reference range (typically 20-40 mg/dL or 0.2-0.4 g/L)
Diagnostic cutoff values (<10 mg/dL highly suggestive, 10-20 mg/dL intermediate)
Acute-phase reactant behavior causing false-negative normal levels during active inflammation or pregnancy
Causes of false-positive low levels (aceruloplasminemia, protein-losing enteropathy, severe hepatic insufficiency, copper deficiency)

cases.question_text: Explain 24-hour urinary copper testing: collection procedure, measurement methods, diagnostic thresholds, and monitoring under chelation therapy.
expected_answer_elements: Specimen collection in a copper-free, acid-washed container over an exact 24-hour window
Analytical measurement methodology and precautions against external environmental contamination

Therapeutic targets during chelator therapy (200-500 µg/24h or 3-8 µmol/24h)
Therapeutic target on zinc maintenance therapy (<75 µg/24h or <1.2 µmol/24h)

cases.question_text: What is the ATP7B gene, where is it located, and what is its role in Wilson disease pathogenesis and familial screening?
expected_answer_elements: Chromosomal localization (chromosome 13q14.3)
Protein function as intracellular transmembrane P-type copper-transporting ATPase (ATPase 2)
Mechanism of cellular defect (impaired copper incorporation into apoceruloplasmin and impaired biliary copper excretion)
Mutation complexity (autosomal recessive, >800 pathogenic variants, frequent compound heterozygosity)
Familial screening protocol for all first-degree relatives (siblings have 25% risk)

cases.question_text: Compare D-penicillamine, trientine, and zinc in treating Wilson disease: mechanism, typical dosage, monitoring, and safety.
expected_answer_elements: D-penicillamine pharmacology (copper chelation promoting urinary excretion; typical dosing 750-1500 mg/day divided)
Trientine pharmacology (chelating agent alternative; preferred in neurological presentation or penicillamine intolerance)
Zinc pharmacology (metallothionein induction blocking intestinal copper absorption; maintenance and presymptomatic dosing)
Comparative efficacy between initial de-coppering and long-term maintenance phases

cases.question_text: What are the major adverse effects of D-penicillamine and trientine, why is Pyridoxine co-prescribed, and what is the danger of abrupt treatment cessation?
expected_answer_elements: Early penicillamine adverse effects (fever, rash, lymphadenopathy, cytopenias, proteinuria)
Late penicillamine toxicities (nephrotic syndrome, lupus-like syndrome, elastosis perforans serpiginosa)
Initial paradoxical neurological worsening (observed in 10-20% on penicillamine initiation)
Trientine adverse effect profile (milder than penicillamine, occasional sideroblastic anemia or worsening)
Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6, 25-50 mg/day) co-administration rationale to prevent antipyridoxine deficiency neuropathy
Critical clinical safety advisory: abrupt cessation risks precipitating fatal acute hepatic failure

cases.question_text: What is the recommended surveillance schedule and laboratory monitoring panel for a Wilson's disease patient on maintenance chelator or zinc therapy?
expected_answer_elements: Surveillance frequency (initial titration: every 1-3 months; stable maintenance: twice yearly to annually)
Routine monitoring laboratory panel (complete blood count, urinalysis, liver biochemistries ALT/AST/bilirubin/INR, renal panel)
24-hour urinary copper assessment intervals and target excretion ranges by drug class
Assessment of adherence, symptom control, and annual slit-lamp exam for Kayser-Fleischer ring resolution

cases.question_text: How should Wilson's Disease be managed during pregnancy, in pediatric patients, and in acute liver failure presentations?
expected_answer_elements: Pregnancy management (therapy must NEVER be stopped; reduce chelator dose by 25-50% in 3rd trimester for wound healing; teratogenicity considerations)
Pediatric considerations (frequent hepatic presentation with asymptomatic transaminitis; zinc monotherapy risk in pediatric liver disease)
Acute liver failure management (rapidly fatal without liver transplantation; utility of King's College or Nazir Prognostic Index; plasma exchange/dialysis bridging)
